previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with metastatic breast cancer and gastroparesis was admitted for abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. She developed acute hypoxia without clear pulmonary cause, leading to transfer to the ICU. Imaging and echocardiography revealed a patent foramen ovale with right-to-left shunting, contributing to hypoxemia. She underwent successful PFO closure, after which her oxygen requirements decreased significantly. Her gastroparesis symptoms were managed with medication adjustments, including a switch to Tigan for nausea. She was also found to have C. difficile colonization without active infection, which did not require treatment. She improved steadily, was weaned off oxygen, and discharged home on aspirin and clopidogrel post-procedure, with follow-up planned in cardiology and gastroenterology.

the Emergency Department after referral by her cardiologist with 
a possible facial droop in the setting of recent PFO closure.

She was recently admitted to ___ ___ through ___ after 
initially presenting with abdominal pain and nausea/vomiting. 
These symptoms were felt to represent a flare of her 
long-standing idiopathic gastroparesis, and she was admitted to 
the medicine floor. However, overnight she became acutely 
hypoxic on the floor with no clear trigger, requiring transfer 
to the ICU. CTA was negative for PE or parenchymal explanation 
for VQ mismatch. TTE showed early bubbles into the left atrium 
consistent with sizable ASD. She was transferred to the CCU for 
further management. PFO closure was performed ___ with good 
response. Aspirin and Plavix were started. She was discharged 
home yesterday. Her husband states that he visited her earlier 
in the day yesterday and did not notice any facial asymmetry.

However, when she arrived home, sometime around 5pm, he thought 
that the left side of her faced seemed somewhat asymmetric, 
especially when she smiled. He states that her speech was clear 
and there was no dysarthria or aphasia, though she did seem to 
be somewhat tired and was taking a bit longer to respond to his
questions than normal. Ms ___ states that she did look in 
the mirror and did not think her face was asymmetric. She was 
able to walk around the house, prepare dinner, shower (including 
washing her hair), and get ready for bed, all without any 
difficulty. All told, her husband thinks the facial droop lasted 
a few hours, and was improving (though perhaps not completely 
resolved) by the
time she went to bed. 

Today, she had a follow up appointment with her cardiologist. 
When her husband mentioned this possible facial droop, she was 
referred to the ED for evaluation. 

On my interview, Ms ___ denies any facial droop, headache, 
vision changes, dysarthria, dysphagia, difficulty speaking or 
comprehending speech, or focal weakness or sensory change. She 
does emphasize that she was very tired last night after her long 
hospitalization. Her husband believes that the facial droop is 
now gone and her face appears normal.

Brief Hospital Course:
Ms ___ is a ___ year old woman with a history of metastatic
breast cancer and recent PFO closure on DAPT, who presented from 
the cardiology office with concern for left facial droop. On 
___, after she was discharged from the hospital following her 
PFO closure, a left facial droop was noticed by her husband but 
not the patient. She had no other symptoms at that time. Given 
her risk factors, she was admitted to the hospital for further 
work-up. 

During her hospital stay, her neurological exam was initially 
notable for left upper motor neuron arm weakness and slow finger 
tapping without evidence of facial droop. Her current exam is 
completely normal. 

Given her metastatic disease and recent PFO closure (which puts 
the patient at risk for new onset atrial fibrillation), she got 
an MRI which showed evidence of osseous metastases and linear 
enhancement overlying left frontal operculum, suspicious for 
metastatic involvement. No acute infarcts were seen. Only risk 
factor labs were notable for LDL of 104. In light of her 
advanced cancer, statins were withheld.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Ms. ___,  
 You were hospitalized due to symptoms of left facial droop 
resulting from an ACUTE ISCHEMIC STROKE, a condition where a 
blood vessel providing oxygen and nutrients to the brain is 
blocked by a clot. The brain is the part of your body that 
controls and directs all the other parts of your body, so damage 
to the brain from being deprived of its blood supply can result 
in a variety of symptoms. 
 
 Stroke can have many different causes, so we assessed you for 
medical conditions that might raise your risk of having stroke. 
In order to prevent future strokes, we plan to modify those risk 
factors. Your risk factors are:  
 High cholesterol
 Recent PFO closure
 Malignancy

 We are changing your medications as follows:  
 *** ?statin

 Please take your other medications as prescribed.  
 Please follow up with Cardiology and your primary care 
physician as listed below.  

 If you experience any of the symptoms below, please seek 
emergency medical attention by calling Emergency Medical 
Services (dialing 911). In particular, since stroke can recur, 
please pay attention to the sudden onset and persistence of 
these symptoms:  
 - Sudden partial or complete loss of vision  
 - Sudden loss of the ability to speak words from your mouth  
 - Sudden loss of the ability to understand others speaking to 
you  
 - Sudden weakness of one side of the body  
 - Sudden drooping of one side of the face  
 - Sudden loss of sensation of one side of the body 
 
 Sincerely,  
 Your ___ Neurology Team

radiology_notes.text:
EXAMINATION:  MR HEAD W AND W/O CONTRAST T___ MR HEAD

INDICATION:  ___ year old woman with metastatic cancer, possible stroke// Eval
for new met and/or stroke

TECHNIQUE:  Sagittal and axial T1 weighted imaging were performed. After
administration of intravenous contrast, axial imaging was performed with
gradient echo, FLAIR, diffusion, and T1 technique. Sagittal MPRAGE imaging was
performed and re-formatted in axial and coronal orientations.

COMPARISON:  CTA of the head neck dated ___.

FINDINGS: 

Well-defined low T1 signal lesions are seen in the C 2, C3, C4 vertebral
bodies, consistent with osseous metastases.

Subtle linear enhancement overlying left frontal operculum series 9, image 14,
series 12, image 12, no associated restricted diffusion, may represent late
subacute cortical infarct, focus of leptomeningeal metastases, inflammatory
process or infection.  No associated abnormality on gradient images.

There is no evidence of hemorrhage, edema, masses, mass effect, midline shift
or infarction.  Brain parenchymal atrophy.  Findings consistent with moderate
chronic small vessel ischemic changes.

There is mild mucosal thickening, secretions of the right sphenoid sinus.  The
intraorbital contents are normal.  There is mild opacification of the
bilateral mastoid air cells.  There is no abnormal enhancement after contrast
administration.  Suggestion of 2 mm right cleft cyst versus pituitary
microadenoma coronal image 77.

IMPRESSION: 

Findings consistent with osseous metastases.
Linear enhancement overlying left frontal operculum, differential
considerations include late subacute infarct, leptomeningeal metastasis,
inflammatory process or infection.
2 mm Rathke's cleft cyst versus microadenoma.
